h1: Porter or stout: is there really a difference between them?
title: Porter vs Stout: The Real Difference | Craft Beer School
desc: Porter and stout share a history and often a taste. Here is where they split, what roasted barley changed and how to tell them apart today.
teaser: Ask ten brewers the difference between porter and stout and you may get ten answers. History gives the honest one.
standfirst: Porter and stout are both dark, roasty beers. Many drinkers cannot tell them apart. That is not a failure of palate. The two styles grew from the same root and have crossed back and forth for three centuries. Here is the history, the modern difference and how to taste it.
sections:
Porter appeared in London in the early eighteenth century. It was a dark, well-hopped brown beer that became hugely popular with the city's working population, including the street and river porters who probably gave it its name. London brewers made it in vast quantities and aged it in huge vats.

Stout began as a description rather than a separate beer. A stronger porter was called stout porter, stout meaning strong or robust. Over time the word porter dropped off. Stout became a style name in its own right. So, historically, a stout was simply a strong porter.

In the nineteenth century, changes in malting technology and in British tax law shaped both beers. The invention of a roasting drum that could produce very dark malt meant brewers could colour their beer with a small amount of black malt instead of using large amounts of brown malt. Later, in Ireland, brewers began using unmalted roasted barley, which gives a sharper, drier, coffee-like roast.

Irish dry stout, with roasted barley, became its own distinct beer: black, dry, with a firm roast bitterness. English porter generally stayed softer and more chocolatey, built on brown and chocolate malts. Porter faded almost completely in Britain in the twentieth century before craft brewers revived it.

Today, if you need a single line: stout tends to be darker, more roasty and fuller in body, often with roasted barley giving a sharp, coffee-like edge. Porter tends to be a little lighter, more chocolatey and more rounded, with less harsh roast. Our porter guide and dry stout guide cover each in depth.

But the rule is loose. A robust porter can be stronger and darker than a dry stout. Some breweries call similar beers by different names out of habit or marketing. The style guidelines overlap. Judges accept that.

English porter. Brown to dark brown, chocolate and toffee flavours, moderate roast, around 4 to 5.5% ABV.

Robust or American porter. Darker, stronger and more roasty, with more hop character.

Baltic porter. A strong, smooth dark lager from the Baltic region, often 7 to 9.5% ABV.

Irish dry stout. Black, dry and roasty, often surprisingly light, around 4 to 4.5% ABV, frequently served on nitrogen for a creamy head.

Sweet, milk and oatmeal stouts. Smoother and sweeter, with lactose or oats for body.

Imperial stout. Big, strong and complex, often 8 to 12% ABV.

The roasted malts carry most of the story. Chocolate malt gives cocoa and coffee notes with softer bitterness. Black malt gives intense colour and a sharper roast. Roasted barley, unmalted, gives the dry, slightly acrid coffee bite that defines Irish dry stout. Our guide to roasted malts explains each one.

A porter brewed mainly with chocolate and brown malts will taste different from a stout built on roasted barley, even at similar strength. That is the clearest practical line between them.

Many people assume dark beer is too heavy for Indian weather. A dry stout at 4.2% is lighter in body and alcohol than most strong lagers on the market. The colour comes from a small amount of roasted grain, not from strength. Dark beers also pair well with Indian food: try a porter with seekh kebabs or a dry stout with a plate of mutton chops. Roast flavours meet char from the grill. The beer's dryness cuts the fat.

The best way to learn is side by side. Pour a porter and a stout at the same temperature, around 10 to 12 °C, into identical glasses. Smell for chocolate and toffee versus coffee and roast. Taste for sweetness, roast bitterness and body. Notice the finish: a dry stout ends sharp and dry, a porter softer and rounder.

Do this a few times with different examples and you will start to recognise the families, while also seeing why brewers themselves argue about the line. Building that kind of structured comparison into your tasting is how palates actually improve.
faqs: Historically, stout meant a stronger porter. Today strength varies widely in both families. A dry stout can be lighter than many porters. Check the ABV.
What gives stout its coffee flavour?
Mostly roasted barley, which is unmalted barley roasted until very dark. It gives a sharp, dry, coffee-like roast, especially in Irish dry stout.
Is dark beer heavier than light beer?
Not necessarily. Colour comes from a small amount of roasted grain. A dry stout around 4.2% ABV is lighter in body and alcohol than many strong lagers.
